about: Authored query pairs on Oracle HR for tools/sample_db_bench.py. label: 'equivalent' or 'different' under the declared keys minus 'drop' (not_null:T.c, pk:T, fk:T.c). A 'different' pair carries a witness: 'real' (the two queries already differ on the HR data) or a small database (missing columns are completed with legal values) that satisfies the remaining declarations and separates them. 'sibling' names the pair it negates.

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: employees.job_id is NOT NULL and references jobs' key: every employee joins exactly one job
pairs.left: SELECT e.employee_id, e.last_name FROM employees AS e JOIN jobs AS j ON e.job_id = j.job_id
pairs.right: SELECT employee_id, last_name FROM employees

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: employees.department_id may be NULL: such an employee joins no department
pairs.left: SELECT e.employee_id, e.last_name FROM employees AS e JOIN departments AS d ON e.department_id = d.department_id
pairs.right: SELECT employee_id, last_name FROM employees

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: without the foreign key an employee may name a job that does not exist
pairs.left: SELECT e.employee_id, e.last_name FROM employees AS e JOIN jobs AS j ON e.job_id = j.job_id
pairs.right: SELECT employee_id, last_name FROM employees

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: without jobs' primary key two jobs may share an id, and the employee joins both
pairs.left: SELECT e.employee_id, e.last_name FROM employees AS e JOIN jobs AS j ON e.job_id = j.job_id
pairs.right: SELECT employee_id, last_name FROM employees

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: a LEFT JOIN on the key of jobs adds no row and no filter
pairs.left: SELECT e.employee_id FROM employees AS e LEFT JOIN jobs AS j ON e.job_id = j.job_id
pairs.right: SELECT employee_id FROM employees

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: an employee with two past jobs appears twice
pairs.left: SELECT e.employee_id FROM employees AS e LEFT JOIN job_history AS jh ON jh.employee_id = e.employee_id
pairs.right: SELECT employee_id FROM employees

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: without jobs' primary key a job id may repeat
pairs.left: SELECT e.employee_id FROM employees AS e LEFT JOIN jobs AS j ON e.job_id = j.job_id
pairs.right: SELECT employee_id FROM employees

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: manager_id references employees' key: an employee with a manager joins exactly that manager, one without joins nobody
pairs.left: SELECT e.employee_id FROM employees AS e JOIN employees AS m ON e.manager_id = m.employee_id
pairs.right: SELECT employee_id FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NOT NULL

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: without the foreign key an employee may name a manager who is not an employee
pairs.left: SELECT e.employee_id FROM employees AS e JOIN employees AS m ON e.manager_id = m.employee_id
pairs.right: SELECT employee_id FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NOT NULL

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: each employee has at most one manager row: the LEFT JOIN to employees' key keeps every employee once
pairs.left: SELECT e.employee_id FROM employees AS e LEFT JOIN employees AS m ON e.manager_id = m.employee_id
pairs.right: SELECT employee_id FROM employees

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: a manager appears once per direct report
pairs.left: SELECT e.employee_id FROM employees AS e LEFT JOIN employees AS r ON r.manager_id = e.employee_id
pairs.right: SELECT employee_id FROM employees

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: job_history.employee_id is NOT NULL and references employees' key
pairs.left: SELECT jh.employee_id, jh.job_id FROM job_history AS jh JOIN employees AS e ON jh.employee_id = e.employee_id
pairs.right: SELECT employee_id, job_id FROM job_history

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: without the foreign key a history row may name an employee that does not exist
pairs.left: SELECT jh.employee_id, jh.job_id FROM job_history AS jh JOIN employees AS e ON jh.employee_id = e.employee_id
pairs.right: SELECT employee_id, job_id FROM job_history

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: the join keeps exactly the employees whose department_id is not NULL (foreign key to the key of departments)
pairs.left: SELECT e.employee_id FROM employees AS e JOIN departments AS d ON d.department_id = e.department_id
pairs.right: SELECT employee_id FROM employees WHERE department_id IS NOT NULL

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: without the foreign key a department_id may name no department
pairs.left: SELECT e.employee_id FROM employees AS e JOIN departments AS d ON d.department_id = e.department_id
pairs.right: SELECT employee_id FROM employees WHERE department_id IS NOT NULL

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: a self join on the whole composite key (employee_id, start_date) matches each row with itself
pairs.left: SELECT a.employee_id, a.job_id FROM job_history AS a JOIN job_history AS b ON a.employee_id = b.employee_id AND a.start_date = b.start_date
pairs.right: SELECT employee_id, job_id FROM job_history

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: employee_id alone is not the key: an employee with two history rows matches twice over
pairs.left: SELECT a.employee_id, a.job_id FROM job_history AS a JOIN job_history AS b ON a.employee_id = b.employee_id
pairs.right: SELECT employee_id, job_id FROM job_history

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: without the primary key two history rows may be identical and match each other
pairs.left: SELECT a.employee_id, a.job_id FROM job_history AS a JOIN job_history AS b ON a.employee_id = b.employee_id AND a.start_date = b.start_date
pairs.right: SELECT employee_id, job_id FROM job_history

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: employee_id is the primary key
pairs.left: SELECT DISTINCT employee_id, last_name FROM employees
pairs.right: SELECT employee_id, last_name FROM employees

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: many employees share a job
pairs.left: SELECT DISTINCT job_id FROM employees
pairs.right: SELECT job_id FROM employees

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: without the primary key two employee rows may be identical
pairs.left: SELECT DISTINCT employee_id, last_name FROM employees
pairs.right: SELECT employee_id, last_name FROM employees

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: (employee_id, start_date) is the primary key and the select list contains it
pairs.left: SELECT DISTINCT employee_id, start_date, job_id FROM job_history
pairs.right: SELECT employee_id, start_date, job_id FROM job_history

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: one employee may hold the same job twice, starting on different dates
pairs.left: SELECT DISTINCT employee_id, job_id FROM job_history
pairs.right: SELECT employee_id, job_id FROM job_history

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: without the primary key a history row may repeat
pairs.left: SELECT DISTINCT employee_id, start_date, job_id FROM job_history
pairs.right: SELECT employee_id, start_date, job_id FROM job_history

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: upstream declares UNIQUE (email), which BigQuery cannot declare and this eval drops: under the declared keys two employees may share an email (the real data has none, so the pair agrees on it)
pairs.left: SELECT DISTINCT email FROM employees
pairs.right: SELECT email FROM employees

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: IN over a subquery is EXISTS of the correlated subquery (NULL department_id matches nothing either way)
pairs.left: SELECT employee_id FROM employees WHERE department_id IN (SELECT department_id FROM departments WHERE location_id = 1700)
pairs.right: SELECT e.employee_id FROM employees AS e WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM departments AS d WHERE d.department_id = e.department_id AND d.location_id = 1700)

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: the subquery selects departments' primary key, so the join cannot repeat an employee
pairs.left: SELECT employee_id FROM employees WHERE department_id IN (SELECT department_id FROM departments WHERE location_id = 1700)
pairs.right: SELECT e.employee_id FROM employees AS e JOIN departments AS d ON e.department_id = d.department_id WHERE d.location_id = 1700

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: without departments' primary key two departments may share an id and the join repeats the employee
pairs.left: SELECT employee_id FROM employees WHERE department_id IN (SELECT department_id FROM departments WHERE location_id = 1700)
pairs.right: SELECT e.employee_id FROM employees AS e JOIN departments AS d ON e.department_id = d.department_id WHERE d.location_id = 1700

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: the subquery selects employees.department_id, which repeats: the join gives one row per employee
pairs.left: SELECT d.department_id FROM departments AS d JOIN employees AS e ON e.department_id = d.department_id WHERE e.salary > 10000
pairs.right: SELECT department_id FROM departments WHERE department_id IN (SELECT department_id FROM employees WHERE salary > 10000)

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: employees.job_id is NOT NULL, so NOT IN cannot be poisoned by a NULL
pairs.left: SELECT job_id FROM jobs WHERE job_id NOT IN (SELECT job_id FROM employees)
pairs.right: SELECT j.job_id FROM jobs AS j WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM employees AS e WHERE e.job_id = j.job_id)

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: departments.manager_id has NULLs: NOT IN then returns no row at all
pairs.left: SELECT employee_id FROM employees WHERE employee_id NOT IN (SELECT manager_id FROM departments)
pairs.right: SELECT e.employee_id FROM employees AS e WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM departments AS d WHERE d.manager_id = e.employee_id)

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: without NOT NULL on employees.job_id one NULL makes NOT IN return nothing
pairs.left: SELECT job_id FROM jobs WHERE job_id NOT IN (SELECT job_id FROM employees)
pairs.right: SELECT j.job_id FROM jobs AS j WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM employees AS e WHERE e.job_id = j.job_id)

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: last_name is NOT NULL
pairs.left: SELECT COALESCE(last_name, 'none') AS n FROM employees
pairs.right: SELECT last_name AS n FROM employees

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: first_name may be NULL
pairs.left: SELECT COALESCE(first_name, 'none') AS n FROM employees
pairs.right: SELECT first_name AS n FROM employees

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: hire_date is NOT NULL
pairs.left: SELECT employee_id FROM employees WHERE hire_date IS NOT NULL
pairs.right: SELECT employee_id FROM employees

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: the president has no manager
pairs.left: SELECT employee_id FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NOT NULL
pairs.right: SELECT employee_id FROM employees

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: email is NOT NULL
pairs.left: SELECT COUNT(email) FROM employees
pairs.right: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: most employees have no commission
pairs.left: SELECT COUNT(commission_pct) FROM employees
pairs.right: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: location_id depends on the grouped primary key department_id
pairs.left: SELECT d.department_id, d.department_name, COUNT(*) AS n FROM departments AS d JOIN employees AS e ON e.department_id = d.department_id GROUP BY d.department_id, d.department_name, d.location_id
pairs.right: SELECT d.department_id, d.department_name, COUNT(*) AS n FROM departments AS d JOIN employees AS e ON e.department_id = d.department_id GROUP BY d.department_id, d.department_name

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: without the primary key two department rows may share id and name but differ in location
pairs.left: SELECT d.department_id, d.department_name, COUNT(*) AS n FROM departments AS d JOIN employees AS e ON e.department_id = d.department_id GROUP BY d.department_id, d.department_name, d.location_id
pairs.right: SELECT d.department_id, d.department_name, COUNT(*) AS n FROM departments AS d JOIN employees AS e ON e.department_id = d.department_id GROUP BY d.department_id, d.department_name

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: job_id is not determined by department_id
pairs.left: SELECT department_id, COUNT(*) AS n FROM employees GROUP BY department_id, job_id
pairs.right: SELECT department_id, COUNT(*) AS n FROM employees GROUP BY department_id

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: a HAVING on the group key is a WHERE
pairs.left: SELECT department_id, COUNT(*) AS n FROM employees GROUP BY department_id HAVING department_id > 50
pairs.right: SELECT department_id, COUNT(*) AS n FROM employees WHERE department_id > 50 GROUP BY department_id

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: a department whose employees all earn 5000 or less has no group on the left and a zero on the right
pairs.left: SELECT department_id, COUNT(*) AS n FROM employees WHERE salary > 5000 GROUP BY department_id
pairs.right: SELECT department_id, COUNTIF(salary > 5000) AS n FROM employees GROUP BY department_id

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: job_id depends on the composite primary key
pairs.left: SELECT employee_id, start_date, COUNT(*) AS n FROM job_history GROUP BY employee_id, start_date, job_id
pairs.right: SELECT employee_id, start_date, COUNT(*) AS n FROM job_history GROUP BY employee_id, start_date

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: without the key the same (employee, start date) may appear with two jobs
pairs.left: SELECT employee_id, start_date, COUNT(*) AS n FROM job_history GROUP BY employee_id, start_date, job_id
pairs.right: SELECT employee_id, start_date, COUNT(*) AS n FROM job_history GROUP BY employee_id, start_date

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: the same job id appears many times
pairs.left: SELECT job_id FROM employees UNION ALL SELECT job_id FROM job_history
pairs.right: SELECT job_id FROM employees UNION DISTINCT SELECT job_id FROM job_history

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: the two filters split the NOT NULL key into two disjoint halves
pairs.left: SELECT employee_id FROM employees WHERE employee_id > 150 UNION ALL SELECT employee_id FROM employees WHERE employee_id <= 150
pairs.right: SELECT employee_id FROM employees

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: salary may be NULL and then matches neither half
pairs.left: SELECT employee_id FROM employees WHERE salary > 5000 UNION ALL SELECT employee_id FROM employees WHERE salary <= 5000
pairs.right: SELECT employee_id FROM employees

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: both job_id columns are NOT NULL
pairs.left: SELECT job_id FROM employees INTERSECT DISTINCT SELECT job_id FROM job_history
pairs.right: SELECT DISTINCT job_id FROM employees WHERE job_id IN (SELECT job_id FROM job_history)

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: INTERSECT matches NULLs, IN does not
pairs.left: SELECT department_id FROM employees INTERSECT DISTINCT SELECT department_id FROM job_history
pairs.right: SELECT DISTINCT department_id FROM employees WHERE department_id IN (SELECT department_id FROM job_history)

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: the filter on the outer side rejects the NULL-padded rows
pairs.left: SELECT e.employee_id, d.department_name FROM employees AS e LEFT JOIN departments AS d ON e.department_id = d.department_id WHERE d.location_id = 1700
pairs.right: SELECT e.employee_id, d.department_name FROM employees AS e JOIN departments AS d ON e.department_id = d.department_id WHERE d.location_id = 1700

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: the filter accepts the NULL-padded row of an employee without a department
pairs.left: SELECT e.employee_id, d.department_name FROM employees AS e LEFT JOIN departments AS d ON e.department_id = d.department_id WHERE d.location_id IS NULL OR d.location_id = 1700
pairs.right: SELECT e.employee_id, d.department_name FROM employees AS e JOIN departments AS d ON e.department_id = d.department_id WHERE d.location_id IS NULL OR d.location_id = 1700

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: a filter on the partition key keeps whole partitions
pairs.left: SELECT employee_id, department_id, r FROM (SELECT employee_id, department_id, salary, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS r FROM employees) AS t WHERE department_id = 50
pairs.right: SELECT employee_id, department_id, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS r FROM employees WHERE department_id = 50

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: filtering before the window removes rows that rank above the kept ones
pairs.left: SELECT employee_id, department_id, r FROM (SELECT employee_id, department_id, salary, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS r FROM employees) AS t WHERE employee_id > 120
pairs.right: SELECT employee_id, department_id, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS r FROM employees WHERE employee_id > 120
